parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish אַכלען (akhlen/akhiln), from Hebrew אָכַל (“(to) eat”).
Borrowed from Yiddish אַשכּנזי (ashkenazi), from Hebrew אַשְׁכְּנַזִּי.

parole.significato: tipster, insider who gives advice to criminals
parole.testo: From Rotwelsch (thieves’ cant), from Yiddish בעלדבר (baldover, “the one in question, the aforementioned”), from Hebrew בעל דבר (baʿal dāvār, literally “lord of the speech”, i.e. “he who is central to the affair”). The sense developed from the use referring to a source whose name one does not want to
Rotwelsch, from Yiddish בית (beys, “house”), itself from Hebrew בַּיִת (báyit). Compare Alemannic German Beiz.

parole.significato: young man who has not yet reached adulthood; youngling, youngster, youth
parole.testo: The word was borrowed via Yiddish בחור (bokher) which in Western Yiddish applied the senses of “boy, youngster, man”, “Talmud student”, especially “Talmud student who gave lessons to Jewish children in exchange for board and lodge”, “teacher of religious education”, “Jewish teacher”, “assistant scho

parole.significato: honorary title given to a distinguished Jewish scholar who is not a rabbi
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish חבֿר (khaver, “friend”), from Hebrew חָבֵר. Doublet of Haberer and Gabber.
Borrowed from Yiddish עצה (eytse) via Rotwelsch, from Hebrew עֵצָה (etsá).

parole.significato: thief, fraudster, member of the criminal underworld, ganef
parole.testo: 19th-century back-formation from the plural Ganoven, from Yiddish גנבֿים (ganóvim), itself plural of גנבֿ (gánev, “thief”), whence the dated German form above. Further from Hebrew גַּנָּב (gannāv).

From thieves’ cant (Rotwelsch) Jauner, Joner (“gambler, cardsharp”), attested ca. 1500 alongside the verb jonen. Further usually derived from Yiddish יוון (Yoven/Yovon, “Greece”), from Hebrew יָוָן (yāwān), because Greeks were said to be skilful cardsharps (compare French Grec in this sense). The an
Borrowed from Yiddish גוי (goy, “Gentile”), from Hebrew גּוֹי (gói, “nation”).
Borrowed from Yiddish גלות (goles), from Hebrew גָּלוּת (galút).

Literally, “to give someone the sour”. However, Saures is not related to sauer (“sour”), but a malapropism of Zores (“tsuris”), from Yiddish צרות (tsores), plural of צרה (tsore, “trouble, problem”), from Hebrew צָרָה (tsará, “trouble, tragedy, calamity”). Compare Dutch sores.
Originally a Rotwelsch term. Borrowed from Yiddish כּפֿר (kafer, “farmer”), from Hebrew כְּפָר (kəp̄ār, “village”).
From Yiddish כּלה (kale, “bride”), from Hebrew כַּלָּה (kalá, “bride”).
Rotwelsch, from Yiddish כּפּרות (kapores), from Hebrew כַּפֹּרֶת (kapporet). Compare Yiddish קאַפּויער (kapoyer, “upside down”). Influenced by kaputt.

parole.significato: to kibitz, to observe curiously, possibly giving unwanted comments, especially at a card game, but also work being done…
parole.testo: From older kiewischen, kiebitschen, meaning “to search, strip-search, investigate” in thieves’ cant (Rotwelsch). Further origin uncertain. Possibly from Yiddish כובש זײַן (koyvesh zayn, “to oppress, distress”), from Hebrew כבש (kāvāš). Later associated with Kiebitz (“lapwing”), but direct derivation
From Rotwelsch (underworld slang), from Yiddish קיס (kis, “pouch”), from Hebrew כיס (kîs), influenced by etymology 1 through association with Steine (“bucks, money”, literally “stones”).
Through Rotwelsch (thieves’ cant) from Yiddish קנס (knas, “a fine”), from Hebrew קְנָס (qənās, “a fine”).

parole.significato: a room in a brothel used for prostitution
parole.testo: Rotwelsch from Yiddish קבה (kove, “bed-chamber”), from Hebrew קֻבָּה (qubbā, “bed-chamber, vaulted tent”) as in Numbers 25:8, akin to Aramaic קוּבְּתָא / ܩܘܼܒ݁ܬ݂ܵܐ (qubbəṯā).
Borrowed from Yiddish כּשר (kosher), from Hebrew כָּשֵׁר (kašér).
Borrowed from Yiddish מחלוקת (makhloykes, “argument, disagreement, dispute”), from Hebrew מַחֲלוֹקֶת (maḥălōqɛṯ, “part, share, argument, disagreement, dispute”).
Rotwelsch, from Yiddish מכולה (mekhule), Hebrew מְכוּלֶה.
Borrowed from Yiddish מכּה (make, “plague, wound”), from Hebrew מַכָּה (maká, “blow, wound”), from הִכָּה (hiká, “to hit, to strike”).
18th century, via Rotwelsch (thieves’ cant) from Yiddish מלאָכה (melokhe, “work, labour”), from Hebrew מְלָאכָה (məlāḵā́, “work, labour”).
Borrowed from Yiddish מזל (mazel, “luck, destiny”), from medieval Hebrew מַזָּל (mazzāl). Related to vermasseln.
Borrowed from Yiddish מצה (matse), from Hebrew מַצָּה (matsá).

parole.significato: a Jew, especially a poor and/or Yiddish-speaking one
parole.testo: From Yiddish משהלע (Moyshele), diminutive of Hebrew משה (Moshe, “Moses”).
Borrowed from Yiddish משפּחה (mishpokhe), in turn from Hebrew משפחה (mishpakhá).
Borrowed from Yiddish מעות (moes), from Hebrew מעות (ma'ot, “coins”). Originally underworld slang.

From Rotwelsch platt machen, platte machen (“to spend the night outside”), originally “to flee outside”, from Yiddish מאַכן פּליטה (makhn pleyte, “to escape, run away”). פּליטה (pleyte) is from Hebrew פְּלֵטָה (pəlēṭā, “remainder, survivors”). Doublet of Pleite.
19th century, via thieves’ cant (Rotwelsch) from Yiddish רוח (reyvakh), from Hebrew רוח (réwaḥ, “profit”).
Borrowed from Yiddish [script needed] (rochus), from Hebrew ברוגז (“angry”).
Borrowed from Yiddish שבת (shabes), from Hebrew שַׁבָּת.

17th century, borrowed from Yiddish סחרן (sakhern, “to do business”), derived from Hebrew סחר (sáḥar, “trade”). The form was influenced by now obsolete schachen (“to plunder”, with long [aː]), itself from Proto-West Germanic *skāk (“robbery”). The synonymous Yiddish שאַכערן (shakhern) may be a rebor

Ultimately from Yiddish שם (shem, “name; reputation”), reinterpreted as “bad reputation, disrepute”, and Yiddish בית (beys, “house”); both from Hebrew שֵׁם (shém, “name”) and Hebrew בית (báyit, “house”). Compare German Beiz.
Borrowed from Yiddish שיכּור (shiker, “drunk”), from Hebrew שיכור / שִׁכּוֹר (shikór, “drunkard”).
Borrowed from Yiddish שמירה (shmire), from Hebrew שמירה (šəmīrā, “guard”). Compare Schmiere stehen.

parole.significato: guard, watch, especially during the perpetration of a crime or otherwise forbidden act
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שמירה (shmire), from Hebrew שמירה (šəmīrā), whence also Austrian German Schmier (“police”).

parole.significato: a cheesy, kitschy film, play or book
parole.testo: 20th century, from now archaic Schmonzes (“idle talk”) + -ette (after Operette or the like). The first component is from Yiddish שמאָנצעס (shmontses), itself likely from Hebrew שְׁמוּעוֹת (šəmūʿōṯ, “rumours”). The alternative form with u probably through (etymologically unfounded) association with s
Borrowed from Yiddish שפֿל (shofl, “shabby”), which is from Hebrew שָׁפָל (šāfāl).
Borrowed from Yiddish שתיקה (shtike), from Hebrew שתיקה (shtika, “silence”), see שָׁתַק (“to be silent”). Compare Dutch stiekem.
Borrowed from Yiddish שטות (shtus, “nonsense”), from Hebrew שְׁטוּת (sh'tút, “nonsense”).
Borrowed from Yiddish תּכלית (takhles, “purpose, result”), from Hebrew תכלית (takhlít, “end, purpose”).
Borrowed from Yiddish טנוף (tinef) (via Rotwelsch), from Hebrew טִנּוּף (tinnúf, “trash”).

parole.significato: the buttocks, rear end, butt, toches
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish תּחת (tokhes, “buttocks”), in turn from Hebrew תַּחַת (tákhat, “buttocks”).
Borrowed from Yiddish טרייף (treyf).
Borrowed from Yiddish צחקען (tskhoken, “to gamble”), from Hebrew שיחק / שִׂחֵק (sikhék, “to play”) or צָחַק (tsakhák, “to laugh”).
Borrowed from Yiddish צרות (tsores), plural of צרה (tsore, “trouble, problem”), from Hebrew צָרָה (tsará, “trouble, tragedy, calamity”).

18th century, spread from Berlin. Borrowed from Yiddish סוס (sus), from Hebrew סוס (sūs). Initial [s] is a (now dated) allophone of /t͡s/ in Berlin and other parts of northern Germany; hence the z-spelling.

Ultimatively from Yiddish חכמה (khokhme, “wisdom, wit, wittiness”), from Hebrew חוכמה (khokhmá, “wisdom”). It is not clear whether the adjective is the past participle of the verb überhochmetzen or the verb hochmetzen with added prefix über-. Compare colloquial Hungarian hochmec.
